issue_context.title: Add Memory support to SendPacketElements
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/ncl See info in area-owners.md if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
## Proposed API ```csharp namespace System.Net.Sockets { public class SendPacketsElement { // Existing APIs: public SendPacketsElement(byte[] buffer); public SendPacketsElement(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count); public SendPacketsElement(byte[] buffer, int offset, int count, bool endOfPacket); public byte[]? Buffer { get; } public int Offset { get; } public int Count { get; } // Proposed APIs: public SendPacketsElement(ReadOnlyMemory buffer); public SendPacketsElement(ReadOnlyMemory buffer, bool endOfPacket); public Memory? MemoryBuffer { get; } } } ``` This is modeled on how we added Memory support to SocketAsyncEventArgs. If you use a new Memory constructor overload, then: - MemoryBuffer will return the Memory that you passed to the constructor - Buffer will return null - Offset will return 0 - Count will return MemoryBuffer.Length If you use an old byte[] constructor overload, then: - MemoryBuffer will return a Memory constructed from the byte[], offset, and count you passed to the constructor. - Buffer, Offset, and Count will return the values you passed to the constructor (as today)
Author: geoffkizer
Assignees: -
Labels: `api-suggestion`, `area-System.Net.Sockets`
Milestone: 6.0.0

> * MemoryBuffer will return a ReadOnlyMemory constructed from the byte[], offset, and count you passed to the constructor.

if this is the case, there's no reason for the `MemoryBuffer` property to be nullable.

> `MemoryBuffer` property to be nullable

Besides that it shouldn't be nullable anyway. If not set, it's `default`, so `IsEmpty` will return `true`.
So to work with the check for `IsEmpty` or `HasValue` has to be done in either way.

But this is superceded by @scalablecory's comment.

> if this is the case, there's no reason for the MemoryBuffer property to be nullable.

SendPacketElements can also be a file (or file segment). In that case, MemoryBuffer will return null, as Buffer does today.

...or MemoyBuffer will just be empty (instead of being null).

For span-overloads if no data is given, they're empty and we don't have nullable spans as arguments where null means void.
Same for other memory-overloads. I see this case in the same vein.

>  I see this case in the same vein.

I think it's different. In this case you're not using a Memory at all; you are using a file.

Ah, ok there it is also nullable, so it should be the same here.
You're right.

review_comments: Rather than storing buffer/offset/count and also storing a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, did you consider just storing the `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`?  If we need the `byte[]` for something (such as if someone accesses the getter), we can use MemoryMarshal.TryGetArray to extract the buffer/offset/count.

It seems slightly weird to me that if you construct it with a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, that you'd be able to get the byte[]/offset/count out of it via the existing properties. I know you can always do this with MemoryMarshal, but that's sort of an advanced API and most people won't ever deal with it.

Note we have to keep the offset/count fields for file cases.

All that said, I don't feel particularly strongly about this.

You could store whether it came from a byte[] in a bool and only give back the array if it did. 

But my motivation here was avoiding increasing the size of the type. If the two ints are needed,  regardless,  meh.
